ego.name: John von Neumann
ego.summary: Hungarian-born American mathematician, physicist, computer scientist, and engineer whose work reshaped set theory, quantum mechanics, game theory, nuclear-weapons research, and stored-program computing. A professor at the Institute for Advanced Study, he connected abstract mathematics with major wartime and postwar technical programs.

connections.relationship_description: Von Neumann’s father was a Budapest banker who encouraged his broad education. Max urged him to gain practical training, and von Neumann studied chemical engineering alongside mathematics.
connections.notes: Max later joined the family migration to the United States in 1939.

connections.relationship_description: Von Neumann's mother raised him in the affluent Kann-Neumann household in Budapest and later followed him to the United States in 1939.
connections.notes: He confided religious reflections to her near the end of his life.

connections.relationship_description: Marina was von Neumann’s only child with his first wife, Marietta Kövesi. She later became an economist, writer, business executive, and professor.
connections.notes: She became an economist, business executive, and professor.

connections.relationship_description: Von Neumann married Dán in Princeton in 1938. She later became one of the first computer programmers and worked on ENIAC and MANIAC I.
connections.notes: Dán worked on ENIAC and MANIAC I and wrote the preface to his posthumously published Silliman Lectures.

connections.relationship_description: Szegő gave von Neumann advanced calculus instruction beginning when von Neumann was 15 and recognized his exceptional mathematical ability immediately.
Von Neumann studied mathematics under Hilbert at the University of Göttingen in 1926-1927 on a Rockefeller Foundation grant.
connections.notes: Hilbert's foundational program formed an important context for von Neumann's early work in logic and set theory.

connections.relationship_description: Wigner was von Neumann’s fellow student at the Fasori Lutheran Gymnasium and became a lifelong friend. They later collaborated in mathematical physics and both built careers in Princeton.
connections.notes: Their friendship linked their early Hungarian education, work in mathematical physics, Princeton careers, and wartime nuclear work.

connections.relationship_description: Morgenstern joined von Neumann in writing Theory of Games and Economic Behavior. Their partnership connected mathematical analysis with economics and strategic decision-making.
connections.notes: Their work joined von Neumann's mathematics to Morgenstern's economics and strategic decision-making.

connections.relationship_description: Von Neumann invited Ulam to the Institute for Advanced Study in 1935; they became close friends and later worked together at Los Alamos on numerical methods, the Monte Carlo method, and nuclear-weapons problems.
connections.notes: Ulam later described a discussion with von Neumann concerning accelerating technological change and a possible historical singularity.

connections.relationship_description: Goldstine met von Neumann at Aberdeen in 1944 and brought him into the EDVAC study group. They subsequently worked together on the Institute for Advanced Study computer project.
connections.notes: Goldstine circulated von Neumann's First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC, which helped make stored-program computer design widely influential.

connections.relationship_description: Bigelow worked with von Neumann on the design of the IAS machine, the stored-program computer project at the Institute for Advanced Study that influenced later computer construction.
connections.notes: Klára Dán von Neumann later programmed the related MANIAC I machine at Los Alamos.

connections.relationship_description: Michael was one of von Neumann's two younger brothers and grew up with him in the Budapest family household.
Nicholas was von Neumann's younger brother and, with other family members, followed him to the United States in 1939.
Von Neumann married Kövesi shortly after his 1930 Catholic baptism; they had one daughter before divorcing in 1937.
connections.notes: Kövesi had studied economics at Budapest University.

connections.relationship_description: Weyl and von Neumann discussed mathematics with Emmy Noether in Göttingen during 1926 and 1927. Weyl later recalled those exchanges.
connections.notes: Weyl's unsuccessful prospective appointment preceded von Neumann's 1933 appointment to the Institute for Advanced Study.

connections.relationship_description: Gödel and von Neumann worked together on foundational questions in set theory, including the continuum hypothesis, and Gödel wrote von Neumann in 1956 about the problem now called P versus NP.
connections.notes: They were also early members of the Institute for Advanced Study faculty.

connections.relationship_description: Mauchly and von Neumann took part in engineering discussions for EDVAC after von Neumann learned of the project in 1944; Mauchly's work on ENIAC and EDVAC informed the computing design debates.
connections.notes: Their connection was consequential but was complicated by disputes over credit for the stored-program concept.

connections.relationship_description: Eckert discussed the planned EDVAC with von Neumann after von Neumann joined the project in 1944-1945, while Eckert was developing its engineering and memory concepts.
connections.notes: Eckert later objected to the attribution implied by the term von Neumann architecture.

connections.relationship_description: Oppenheimer directed the Los Alamos Laboratory during the Manhattan Project, where von Neumann contributed hydrodynamic and shock-wave calculations for implosion weapons from 1943 to 1945.
connections.notes: Their relationship placed von Neumann's applied mathematics within the wartime atomic-bomb program.

connections.relationship_description: Von Neumann worked alongside Schriever and Trevor Gardner on the design and development of the first United States intercontinental ballistic missile programs in the 1950s.
Von Neumann worked alongside Gardner and Bernard Schriever on early United States intercontinental ballistic missile programs during the 1950s.

category_summaries.summary: Von Neumann’s family gave him an affluent Budapest upbringing and expected practical achievement as well as intellectual distinction. Max von Neumann directed him toward chemical engineering alongside mathematics. His parents and brothers joined the family migration to the United States in 1939. His first marriage produced his only child, Marina, and his marriage to Klára Dán later connected his Princeton household to early electronic computing.

Mathematical teachers, classmates, and collaborators carried von Neumann from Budapest and Göttingen to Princeton. Gábor Szegő and David Hilbert trained him in advanced mathematics. Wigner, Weyl, Gödel, and Morgenstern linked his work to physics, logic, and economics. The partnership with Morgenstern produced Theory of Games and Economic Behavior in 1944.

The computing circle around von Neumann began with the EDVAC discussions in Philadelphia. Herman Goldstine connected him with the engineers building EDVAC, and John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert contributed to the design debates. At the Institute for Advanced Study, Julian Bigelow and Goldstine worked with him on the IAS machine. The EDVAC report helped spread stored-program computer design and also led to disputes over credit.

Defense work put von Neumann’s mathematics into United States weapons and missile programs. At Los Alamos he calculated explosive effects for implosion weapons. In the 1950s, Bernard Schriever and Trevor Gardner worked with him on early intercontinental-ballistic-missile programs. He also served on the Atomic Energy Commission and Defense Department committees.
